title: Martha Deserves More Credit Than She Gets
paragraphs:
Martha Deserves More Credit Than She Gets
The Disciple We Criticized, The Woman Jesus Never Condemned, and the Forgotten Beauty of Faithful Service
Most people know Martha for one moment.
And because of that, generations of Christians have quietly placed her in a category she never deserved.
The woman who got it wrong.
The sister who should have been more like Mary.
But what if we've been reading Martha too quickly?
What if one of the most misunderstood women in Scripture has been unfairly reduced to her worst moment?
What if the woman many believers criticize is actually one of the most courageous, faithful, and theologically profound followers of Jesus in the entire New Testament?
Because when you slow down and look closely, Martha's story becomes something far deeper than a lesson about busyness.
It becomes a story of devotion.
A story that proves once again that from scandal to grace, Jesus rewrites everything.
The account most people remember comes from Luke 10:38-42.
Jesus enters the home of Martha and Mary.
"Now as they went on their way, Jesus entered a village. And a woman named Martha welcomed Him into her house." (Luke 10:38)
The house is identified with Martha.
In a first-century culture where women rarely possessed social authority, Martha appears to be the head and host of the household.
She is the one welcoming Jesus.
She is the one carrying responsibility.
She is the one making sure everyone is fed.
She is serving the Son of God.
The Greek word used in Luke 10:40 is διακονία (diakonia).
It is often translated as "service" or "ministry."
Ironically, this is the same root from which we derive the concept of deacons and Christian ministry.
She was trying to honor Jesus.
Mary sits at Jesus' feet listening to His teaching.
Anyone who has ever carried responsibility while others seemed free understands that feeling.
The work still needs to be done.
"Lord, do You not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her then to help me." (Luke 10:40)
It's harder to admit we've sounded exactly like her.
Most of us have prayed some version of that prayer.
Lord, why am I carrying this alone?
Lord, why does nobody see what I'm doing?
Behind Martha's frustration is something deeply human.
And Jesus responds with one of the gentlest corrections in Scripture.
"Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary." (Luke 10:41-42)
Notice what Jesus does not say.
He does not say serving is bad.
He does not say work is bad.
He does not say hospitality is bad.
He does not rebuke her love.
The Greek word translated "anxious" is μεριμνᾷς (merimnas), carrying the idea of being pulled apart in different directions.
Her problem was that her heart had become divided.
He was rescuing her from worry.
Yet for centuries, Martha became the symbol of what not to be.
Because her story doesn't end there.
The brother Martha loved is gone.
And where do we find Martha?
"When Martha heard that Jesus was coming, she went and met Him." (John 11:20)
While everyone else is drowning in grief, Martha walks directly toward the One she still trusts.
And then comes one of the most extraordinary conversations in the entire Bible.
"Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died." (John 11:21)
"But even now I know that whatever You ask from God, God will give You." (John 11:22)
Two words carrying mountains of faith.
"I am the resurrection and the life." (John 11:25)

Ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ἀνάστασις καὶ ἡ ζωή
(Egō eimi hē anastasis kai hē zōē)
"I AM the resurrection and the life."
The phrase Ἐγώ εἰμι (Egō eimi) intentionally echoes God's self-revelation.
Jesus is not merely offering comfort.
He is revealing His divine identity.
And then He asks Martha a question.
Her answer should be discussed far more often than Peter's confession.
"Yes, Lord; I believe that You are the Christ, the Son of God, who is coming into the world." (John 11:27)
Think about what Martha just declared.
Jesus had not yet gone to the cross.
The resurrection had not yet occurred.
The empty tomb was still ahead.
And yet Martha publicly confessed that Jesus was the Messiah, the Son of God.
One of the clearest Christ-centered confessions in all four Gospels comes not from a king.
The woman many people remember only for being busy.
How many believers today can relate to her?
And sometimes you've wondered whether anybody sees it.
The beautiful truth of the Gospel is that Jesus never freezes people in their worst moment.
That's why the Gospel changes everything.
The Samaritan woman had a broken past.
Mary Magdalene carried a painful history.
And Martha had an overwhelmed moment.
Yet Jesus transformed every one of their stories.
Maybe you've spent years feeling like the "Martha" in your family.
The one wondering if your faithfulness matters.
"For God is not unjust so as to overlook your work and the love that you have shown for His name."
Nothing done for Christ is wasted.
And perhaps that is why Martha deserves far more credit than she gets.
Because she teaches us something many modern believers desperately need to remember.
Faith is not only found sitting at Jesus' feet.
Faith is also found serving Him faithfully when nobody applauds.
Ordinary places where ordinary believers keep loving Jesus.
The Kingdom of God advances not only through preachers and teachers but also through countless Marthas whose names may never become famous this side of eternity.
And when Heaven tells Martha's story, it won't be defined by one anxious afternoon.
It will be defined by a woman who opened her home to Christ, served Him with devotion, ran to Him in grief, confessed Him as Messiah, and trusted Him even when death seemed final.
Maybe that's why her story still reaches into our hearts today.
Because deep down, many of us are Martha.
And discovering that Jesus loves us enough to correct us without rejecting us.
The same Savior who gently spoke, "Martha, Martha," is still speaking today.
The kind of grace that turns exhausted servants into faithful witnesses.
The kind of grace that transforms ordinary people into eternal testimonies.
The kind of grace that rewrites every story surrendered to Him.
Your testimony may encourage someone else who is barely holding on.
If these Christ-centered articles strengthen your faith, help us continue sharing biblical truth that points people to Jesus.
One day you may discover that the chapter you were most embarrassed by became the chapter Jesus used to reveal His glory.
